summary: Sets out the IESG's policy on character sets and languages in Internet protocols, to guide standardization work in the IETF. Among its requirements is support for UTF-8. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2277 sets IETF policy for text in Internet protocols. It requires protocols to identify character encodings, support UTF-8, and provide a way to identify the language of text.

questions: what is the ietf policy on character sets
do ietf protocols have to support utf-8
what is the i-default language tag
subtitle: The IETF policy for character encodings and language information in protocols.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols carry text used by people across many languages, but protocols need consistent rules for identifying character encodings and language.
tldr.mechanism: The policy requires protocols to identify the charset of character data, support UTF-8, and provide a way to carry language information. Protocols that present text to users must support multiple languages.
tldr.outcome: The document records IESG policy for IETF standards work. A protocol that cannot support UTF-8 needs a justified variance to enter or advance on the standards track.

today: RFC 2277 is a Best Current Practice published in January 1998. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: International Text in Internet Protocols
sections.content:
The Internet connects people who use many languages and writing systems. This document records the policies that the Internet Engineering Steering Group applies to standardization work in the IETF.

The policy is based on recommendations from the IAB Character Set Workshop. Its requirements apply to protocols submitted to the IETF standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet protocols carry text for people who use different languages. This document sets rules to help protocols represent and identify that text.

sections.title: Where Internationalization Applies
sections.content:
Internationalization applies to text strings, not to protocol commands themselves. When protocol elements resemble text tokens, a specification must identify which parts are commands and which parts are text.

The policy does not dictate how names are internationalized. Each protocol must say whether names use internationalized forms or US-ASCII, and a working group must ensure that any other layer given responsibility knows that it has that responsibility.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol must distinguish machine commands from text that people read. Its specification must also say how names are represented.

sections.title: Character Sets and UTF-8
sections.content:
A charset is a set of rules for mapping octets to characters. Protocols must identify the charset used for all character data and must be able to use UTF-8 for all text.

A protocol may also support other charsets or encodings, including UTF-16. Any additional charset must be registered with IANA if needed. A protocol that cannot use UTF-8 violates this policy and needs a clear justification through the variance procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol message containing character data must identify its encoding. Protocols must support UTF-8, though they may support additional registered encodings.

sections.title: Choosing a Character Set
sections.content:
When a protocol allows more than one charset, the sender and recipient need a way to decide which one applies. If they communicate directly, they may negotiate the choice before sending data.

For stored data or messages without direct negotiation, the charset should be clearly labelled and should be widely understood. Text cannot be read correctly by software that does not support its charset.
sections.plainLanguage: When a protocol allows several encodings, it must make clear which one a message uses. Directly communicating parties may negotiate the choice; stored data needs a clear label.

sections.title: Language Tags and Language Choice
sections.content:
Protocols that transfer text must provide a defined way to carry information about its language. They should also provide language information for names where appropriate. The policy recommends RFC 1766 language tags.

Protocols that display text to users in response to their actions must support multiple languages. When the sender does not know the recipient's language preference, text should use the Default Language tag i-default and must be understandable by an English-speaking person.
sections.plainLanguage: Text needs a language label so software can present and process it appropriately. If a protocol shows text to users, it must support more than one language and provide a default for cases where preferences are unknown.

sections.title: Locale and Documenting Decisions
sections.content:
A POSIX locale identifies cultural conventions such as sorting order, date format, and currency format. The policy encourages protocols to carry locale information when it helps, but does not require it for all text. The default locale is POSIX.

Specifications that address internationalization should collect their decisions in an Internationalization considerations section next to Security Considerations. The RFC notes that foreign-language security warnings and inconsistent language variants can affect security.
sections.plainLanguage: A locale describes conventions such as date and currency formats; it is different from a language tag. Protocol specifications should summarize their internationalization choices so implementers can find them.
